who: Jack P. Maddex, historian of the nineteenth-century United States at the University of Oregon; PhD UNC Chapel Hill, 1966.

evidence.says: Oregon identifies Jack Maddex as history professor emeritus, PhD UNC Chapel Hill 1966, on its faculty since 1966; his publications include The Virginia Conservatives, 1867-1879 (1970).
The history faculty list gives his name as Jack P. Maddex and repeats the North Carolina doctorate in 1966.
The candidate authority cites The Virginia Conservatives, 1867-1879 (1970), whose title page names Jack P. Maddex, Jr.

notes: The university career, exact doctorate, and shared book establish the match to the LC-backed candidate.

who: Stuart George McCook, historian of tropical agriculture and environmental history at Guelph; PhD Princeton, 1996.

evidence.says: Guelph lists a Princeton history PhD in 1996 and an associate professorship at Guelph from 2003 to 2018, covering both students in 2013.
The 1996 graduates include Stuart McCook, author of The Agricultural Awakening of Latin America: Science, Development, and Nature 1900-1930.
The authority for Stuart George McCook cites The Agricultural Awakening of Latin America (1996), with that full name on its title page.

notes: The dissertation connects the LC full-name identity to the Princeton graduate and Guelph faculty member.

who: James Lee McDonough, historian of the American Civil War and professor emeritus of history at Auburn University.

evidence.says: University of Tennessee Press identifies James Lee McDonough as a professor of history at Auburn and author of Five Tragic Hours and Stones River.
The publisher names James Lee McDonough as the author of Five Tragic Hours and identifies him as Auburn history professor emeritus.
The James L. McDonough authority includes the variant James Lee McDonough and cites Five Tragic Hours (1983), whose title page uses the full name.

notes: The same book and full-name variant connect the candidate directly to the Auburn historian. The 1966 Florida State doctorate was not independently verified.

who: Elizabeth Ann McDougall, historian of the Sahara and North/West Africa at Alberta since 1986; PhD Birmingham, 1980.

evidence.says: Her institutional CV gives Elizabeth Ann McDougall, BA Toronto 1975, PhD Birmingham 1980 on the Ijil salt industry, and an Alberta appointment beginning in 1986.
The candidate authority is Elizabeth Ann Kerr McDougall, identified from Selected Correspondence of the Glasgow Colonial Society 1825-1840 (1994).
The Dictionary of Canadian Biography identifies Elizabeth Ann Kerr McDougall as formerly a freelance historian in Westmount, Quebec.
An article by Elizabeth Ann Kerr McDougall cites E. A. Kerr McDougall, The Presbyterian Church in Western Lower Canada, 1815-1842, a McGill PhD thesis from 1969.
McGill lists Elizabeth Ann McDougall as author of that Presbyterian Church dissertation, PhD 1969.

notes: The candidate is the historian of Canadian church history associated with a McGill doctorate in 1969; the supervisor has a different educational chronology and a Birmingham doctorate on Saharan history.

who: Tracy Neumann, urban and public historian at Wayne State University during the students’ doctoral years; PhD NYU.

evidence.says: This ORCID names Tracy Neumann and lists Overpromising Technocracy’s Potential: The American-Yugoslav Project, Urban Planning, and Cold War Cultural Diplomacy, DOI 10.1177/15385132211060041.
The publication metadata names Tracy Neumann, gives the exact candidate ORCID, and identifies her affiliation as Department of History, Wayne State University.
The Urban History Association interview identifies her as Wayne State associate professor of history; she states that she obtained her doctorate and current job in 2011.
The project biography identifies Wayne State public history coordinator Tracy Neumann and states that she earned her history PhD at New York University.

notes: The ORCID-to-publication-to-Wayne State link establishes identity. Her own account gives 2011 for the doctorate, versus 2010 in the supplied AHA record.

who: Peter Nesbitt Oliver, York University historian of Ontario political, social, and legal history.

evidence.says: York identifies Peter Nesbitt Oliver as its Canadian history professor emeritus, specializing in Ontario history; he edited the Ontario Historical Studies Series during 1971-1993.
The Peter Oliver authority cites Unlikely Tory (1985) and records Peter N. Oliver and Peter Oliver as forms of the same author’s name.
York’s archives describe interviews with historian Peter Oliver for Unlikely Tory: The Life and Politics of Allan Grossman (1985).

notes: The authority’s name variants and Ontario-history book agree with the York historian. The Toronto doctorate year was not independently verified.

who: Otto H. Olsen, historian of Reconstruction, visiting professor at Wisconsin–Madison in 1966-67 from Morgan State College.

evidence.says: Wisconsin lists Olsen, Otto as adviser of David Overy’s Robert Lewis Dabney dissertation and Joaquin Cardoso’s Hinton Rowan Helper dissertation in 1966-1967.
A university news release dated October 14, 1966 identifies Otto H. Olsen in Madison’s history department as a visiting professor from Morgan State College that year.
Hopkins Press identifies Otto H. Olsen, author of the Reconstruction-era biography Carpetbagger’s Crusade, with Morgan State College’s history department.
The authority identifies Otto H. Olsen as author of The Ku Klux Klan: A Study in Reconstruction Politics and Propaganda (1962).

notes: The university’s adviser list and contemporary release establish the full-name identity and exact period. The Johns Hopkins doctorate year was not independently verified.

who: Denis George Paz, historian of British education and religious history at North Texas; PhD Michigan, 1974.

evidence.says: The 2010-2011 UNT graduate catalogue lists Denis George Paz as professor of history, with a PhD from the University of Michigan.
Michigan’s history newsletter identifies Denis Paz, PhD 1974, as a North Texas history professor and author of Dickens and Barnaby Rudge.
The D. G. Paz authority cites The Politics of Working-Class Education in Britain, 1830-50 (1980), with Denis G. Paz as an expanded form.
UNT’s departmental book catalogue lists Denis G. Paz as author of The Politics of Working-Class Education in Britain, 1830-50 and Dickens & Barnaby Rudge.

notes: The full name, exact Michigan doctorate year, North Texas affiliation, and overlapping works connect the supervisor to the LC candidate.
